"Carlos Fonseca" explained to him, the original had been lost, so they decided to look for the one closest to the sequence —taken a second before or after the other— to replace it. "It was almost the same, only in this one I had a lost look," he recommended, referring to the ideas of Desiderius Erasmus in "De copia" and "De ratio studii." His method was to make notes on whatever he was reading, categorized by theme: he carted these commonplaces in boxes that accompanied him. When assembling a new book, he would go through the topics and cross out commonplace notes as he used them.

He demonstrated the reason for the inclusion of the Greek text when defending his work: "But one thing the facts cry out, and it can be clear, as they say, even to a blind man, that often through the translator's clumsiness or inattention the Greek has been wrongly rendered; often the Latin, too, has been mauled in the same way."

Jorge Luis Borges claimed that Juan Rulfo's character Pedro Páramo could "recite the whole book, forwards and backwards." Borges considered Pedro Páramo to be one of the greatest texts written in any language.

The narrative structure of Pedro Páramo is unique. The story begins with the first-person account of Juan Preciado, who promises to fulfill his mother's dying wish to find his father, Pedro Páramo, in the Mexican village of Comala. However, as the narrative progresses, it becomes clear that Juan Preciado is not only recounting his own experiences but also those of the other characters, both living and dead. The story blends elements of reality and fantasy, creating a haunting and dreamlike atmosphere.
